questions.q: What are the four recurring activities of an AI manager?
options: Scoping, team leadership, risk and governance, delivery and iteration
questions.explain: It turns an AI capability into something that ships and delivers a measurable outcome.

questions.q: What is NOT the AI manager's job?
options: Personally writing training code, tuning hyperparameters or building pipelines
questions.explain: They need enough understanding to ask good questions and catch bad answers.

questions.q: What does scoping mean?
options: Translating a vague ask like 'use AI to reduce churn' into a specific, testable problem
questions.explain: It's where the project is made testable.

questions.q: Why does the lesson distinguish AI PM, AI engineering manager and AI program manager?
options: Job postings use them interchangeably but accountabilities differ, and a mismatch surfaces painfully around month three
questions.explain: The AI PM owns what gets built and why.

questions.q: What are the three flavours of 'AI' a manager handles?
options: Classical ML, deep learning/vision/traditional NLP, and LLMs/GenAI
questions.explain: Each has different cost, risk and timeline.

questions.q: What is the most common management mistake here?
options: Treating all three as interchangeable 'AI projects' with the same estimation rules
questions.explain: An LLM demo can look finished in an afternoon yet be months from production-safe.

questions.q: Which can ship quickly despite being unglamorous?
options: A classical ML model on tabular data, in about three weeks
questions.explain: Ask which category you're in before promising a date.

questions.q: Why learn the build stages?
options: To ask sharp questions and tell 'needs more data' from 'needs a different approach'
questions.explain: Data collection, training, evaluation, and so on each have things to watch.

questions.q: How does an AI project lifecycle differ from a normal feature build?
options: It loops and can dead-end for legitimate reasons, with phase durations hard to predict
questions.explain: Seven stages from problem framing to monitoring and iteration.

questions.q: A proof of concept shows the approach doesn't work. Is the project a failure?
options: No: it did its job of preventing a more expensive stage-5 failure
questions.explain: Stages 3 and 4 are expected to sometimes fail or reset.

questions.q: What are kill criteria?
options: Explicit conditions to stop, budgeted at the end of stages 1–3
questions.explain: Don't treat every project as guaranteed to reach launch.

questions.q: What is the manager's key question at launch?
questions.explain: Launch is often gradual.

questions.q: Which standard engineering habits can backfire for ML teams?
options: Sprint velocity, story points and 'done means shipped'
questions.explain: Research-like work is less predictable.

questions.q: How do the data scientist and ML engineer differ?
options: Data scientists explore data and build/evaluate models with statistical rigor; ML engineers turn validated models into reliable production code
questions.explain: They're distinct skill sets.

questions.q: Who typically manages these teams, per the lesson?
options: People from general software engineering or product backgrounds, applying habits that don't fit
questions.explain: Adjust structure, planning rhythm and evaluation.

questions.q: What should the structure ensure?
options: Roles are clear so nothing falls through the cracks
questions.explain: For example between research and productionisation.

questions.q: When does AI ethics catch almost nothing?
options: When built in from the start
When bolted on after the model already exists as an afterthought or legal checkbox
questions.explain: Handle it as a management discipline from the start.

questions.q: Which are the five responsible-AI principles listed?
options: Fairness, transparency, accountability, privacy and safety
questions.explain: Each comes with a management question to ask.

questions.q: Where does bias usually come from?
options: The data or problem framing before modelling starts: historical, sampling and label bias
questions.explain: Knowing sources lets you ask early.

questions.q: Example of historical bias?
options: Training data reflecting past discriminatory decisions, such as historical hiring
questions.explain: Sampling bias is data unrepresentative of the real population.

questions.q: What is the most common source of AI project failure per the lesson?
options: A good model promised on a bad timeline to a stakeholder never told uncertainty is legitimate
questions.explain: 'We don't know exactly how long' is a professional answer.

questions.q: How should timelines be communicated?
options: A range tied to explicit checkpoints where it narrows
questions.explain: Kickoff wide, pre-launch a firm evidence-backed date.

questions.q: How does an AI estimate differ from 'this feature takes 3 weeks'?
options: 'The proof of concept takes 3 weeks; whether it's viable to proceed is decided then'
questions.explain: Effort can be dominated by one unknown such as data quality.

questions.q: What does missing a quality bar mean in AI?
options: The approach may not be achievable, not just 'not done yet'
questions.explain: That's why uncertainty must be acknowledged up front.

questions.q: Why not decide purely on a vendor demo?
options: Demos run on best-case examples; quality is probabilistic and hard to verify
questions.explain: Ask for a pilot on a sample of your own data.

questions.q: What pricing should you check?
options: The cost model at your actual expected volume, not the entry tier
questions.explain: Scale changes the economics.

questions.q: What should you ask about data handling?
options: Where it's processed and stored, and whether it's used to train their model
questions.explain: Also privacy terms.

questions.q: What latency and reliability evidence do you need?
options: Real p95/p99 latency numbers and an uptime SLA
questions.explain: Also check lock-in risk: how hard it is to switch later.

questions.q: What does 'model drift' mean in business terms?
options: The system's real-world performance has started slipping as customer behaviour or data changes
questions.explain: Translate jargon before the meeting.

questions.q: What is the 'confidence, not certainty' habit?
options: Never let stakeholders believe an AI system is more reliable than it is; state performance as a rate with real consequences
questions.explain: Instead of 'the model is 90% accurate', say about 9 of 10 are handled correctly and what happens to the other one.

questions.q: What is wrong with oversimplifying?
questions.explain: Too technical makes them tune out or approve what they didn't understand.

questions.q: How do you explain 'we need more labeled data'?
options: We need more examples of correct answers to teach the system from
questions.explain: Keep a translation table handy.

questions.q: Which are core AI risk categories?
options: Bias, hallucination, security/adversarial, privacy leakage, overreliance and model drift
questions.explain: They don't disappear because a model tests well.

questions.q: What is overreliance (automation complacency)?
options: Humans stop critically reviewing AI output because it's usually right
questions.explain: Design review steps to counter it.

questions.q: How should risk be scored?
options: By impact if wrong and reversibility
questions.explain: A lending decision needs far more rigour than a low-stakes internal tool.

questions.q: What is a prompt-injection-style attack?
options: Inputs deliberately crafted to manipulate the model's output
questions.explain: It falls under security/adversarial risk.

questions.q: Why write a charter before work starts?
options: Scoping, ethics, expectations, vendor and risk decisions are cheap to change before building
questions.explain: A half-day charter can save weeks of rework.

questions.q: What does the problem-statement section require?
options: A one-sentence jargon-free problem, AI category, success metric, minimum threshold and a non-AI baseline
questions.explain: The baseline shows what a simple approach achieves.

questions.q: Which role owns the response if the model causes harm after launch?
questions.explain: Named in the roles table.

questions.q: What does the build-versus-buy section ask?
options: Is it core to differentiation, and does a vendor meet the bar on our own data?
questions.explain: The recommendation is build, buy or hybrid.

questions.q: What do most ML team days consist of?
options: Running experiments to find out which model is worth building
questions.explain: Managers control the structure around experiments.

questions.q: What determines whether the team converges or wanders?
options: Structure: what counts as a result, the success bar, tracking and decision rules
questions.explain: Managers rarely read training curves themselves.

questions.q: Why define a success bar before experiments?
options: So the team knows when to stop or switch approach
questions.explain: Otherwise iteration never ends.

questions.q: What should be tracked for experiments?
options: Configurations, data versions and results, so they're reproducible and comparable
questions.explain: Reproducibility matters.

questions.q: What are the three layers of AI metrics?
questions.explain: Insist every project names at least one per layer and how movement propagates down.

questions.q: Which two questions expose most metric problems?
options: 'Compared to what?' and 'what does that cost us in dollars?'
questions.explain: Baselines and cost bridge the scoreboards.

questions.q: What do precision and recall mean?
options: Precision: of flagged items, what share were right; recall: of the real items, what share were caught
questions.explain: They trade off; the balance is a business decision.

questions.q: How can a model get better while the product gets worse?
options: Higher offline accuracy can surface less diverse results and reduce engagement
questions.explain: Most dysfunction lives between model and product layers.

questions.q: Why does MLOps lose roadmap arguments?
options: It's invisible when working, so it loses to visible features until the first incident, then gets funded in a panic at three times the price
questions.explain: Defend the investment before the incident.

questions.q: What is the manager reflex when the team asks for MLOps investment?
options: Make them name the job and the failure it prevents
questions.explain: 'We can't reproduce the model behind a disputed March decision' gets funded; 'we need a feature store' is only a solution.

questions.q: Which are among the seven MLOps jobs?
options: Data pipelines, reproducibility, versioning, deployment, monitoring, retraining, governance and audit
questions.explain: Each has different costs.

questions.q: Most orgs claiming to be level 3 on the maturity model are really...
questions.explain: Locate the team honestly.

questions.q: What is data governance, in the lesson's framing?
options: A committee that slows things down
A set of pre-made decisions about who may do what with which data
questions.explain: Made in advance they cost hours; during an incident, weeks.

questions.q: Which five questions does governance answer?
options: Who owns it, who may use it and for what, where it came from, how good it is, how long we may keep it
Who built it, when, where, why, how
questions.explain: If you can't answer them you have a policy document, not governance.

questions.q: Why is the purpose question the one AI work breaks most often?
options: Data collected to deliver a service isn't automatically data you may train on; it's a different purpose that may need a different legal basis
questions.explain: It's the most common reason a finished model can't ship.

questions.q: Why is deletion harder for AI?
options: A pattern learned from a row is much harder to remove than the row; 'we'll retrain' can mean six weeks and re-validation
questions.explain: Governance matters once data is copied into a model.

questions.q: Which five functions does a consequential AI initiative need?
options: Data science, engineering, product, legal/compliance and design
questions.explain: Each has a different definition of done.

questions.q: What is the manager's job with disagreements?
options: Make them happen early, in a named forum, with a named decider
questions.explain: Not late in a Slack thread with everyone assuming someone else decided.

questions.q: What's 'done' for data science versus engineering?
options: Data science: a metric clears a bar; engineering: it survives production
questions.explain: Legal: risk documented and accepted; design: a person can use it without being misled.

questions.q: What failure does treating them as one team cause?
options: A mismatch in 'done' discovered at integration time
questions.explain: Name the forum and decider upfront.

questions.q: What are the four options, not two?
questions.explain: 'Buy and wrap' is where most current AI work sits.

questions.q: Why is the decision costly to reverse?
options: A built system carries permanent maintenance; a bought one embeds a dependency whose switching costs compound; you choose for about three years
questions.explain: Strategy narrows the field, cost breaks the tie, diligence protects you.

questions.q: What does 'buy and wrap' mean?
options: A vendor model or API underneath, with your own orchestration, data, evaluation and UX on top; budget it as engineering
questions.explain: The model itself is replaceable.

questions.q: Why ask for the 'don't' heuristic's number in week one?
options: After six weeks of vendor evaluation it's psychologically hard to conclude a three-rule heuristic captures 70% of the value
questions.explain: Keep 'don't' a real option throughout.

questions.q: Why do AI principles often change no decisions?
options: A principle without a gate attached is a poster
questions.explain: The gap is a process gap.

questions.q: What is the test of whether an organisation does responsible AI?
options: Whether it can name something it decided not to ship, and why
questions.explain: It needs a gate with a person who can say no.

questions.q: Which framework does the lesson suggest as the internal spine?
options: NIST AI RMF, structured as activities that map onto a delivery process
questions.explain: EU AI Act is a compliance obligation; ISO 42001 optional assurance.

questions.q: Do sector rules matter?
options: Yes: they usually bind harder than anything AI-specific; 'it's AI' is a new way to breach an old regime
questions.explain: Model-risk governance and discrimination law already apply.

questions.q: What's the most expensive AI failure?
options: A model that works and ships but is quietly ignored
questions.explain: The missing metric is the fraction of intended users using it weekly.

questions.q: Why is AI adoption harder than ordinary software adoption?
options: Probabilistic output, it changes the work itself (authors become editors/reviewers), and it carries an unspoken job-survival question
questions.explain: Answer the job question or people answer it pessimistically.

questions.q: What are the adoption funnel stages?
options: Aware, able, activated, repeating, relying, right-sized trust
questions.explain: Each stage has a different failure and fix.

questions.q: What does 'adoption is a budget line and a design constraint' mean?
options: It must be planned and funded, not left to a launch email
questions.explain: Measure usage and business movement.

questions.q: Where does AI budgeting break the headcount model?
options: Part of the cost is usage-driven and scales with success, and the front of the project is genuinely unpredictable
questions.explain: You're buying an answer to 'is this feasible at acceptable quality'.

questions.q: What is the way out of the twelve-month-number trap?
options: Staged funding in tranches tied to decision points, plus honest unit economics
questions.explain: Teams are asked to commit at the moment they know least.

questions.q: What's the most common budgeting error?
options: Building the plan around modelling work, usually the smallest line
questions.explain: Model all cost categories.

questions.q: What do you need so finance understands the economics?
options: Which costs grow when the product succeeds (unit economics)
questions.explain: Usage-driven costs scale with success.

questions.q: Why is writing the MLOps process a manager's job?
options: It's mostly decision rights and thresholds, must be proportionate to portfolio risk, and will be defended in a budget conversation
questions.explain: The deliverable is four pages.

questions.q: What four things does the document cover?
options: Experiment tracking, deployment gates, monitoring and response, evidence retention
questions.explain: Plus a scope-and-tiers section.

questions.q: Which rule makes the document used rather than quoted ironically?
options: Every threshold is a number, not an adjective
questions.explain: Resist writing a policy; specificity is the value.

questions.q: What are the symptoms of not having it?
options: Every release negotiated from scratch, incidents investigated by whoever remembers, audits as archaeology
questions.explain: Shared understanding evaporates when people leave.

questions.q: Past roughly how many people does shared context break down silently?
questions.explain: Symptoms look unrelated: duplicated feature work, incompatible eval sets.

questions.q: What is the symptom at about 25–30 ICs in multiple pods?
options: Pods duplicate infrastructure (two feature stores, two eval harnesses)
questions.explain: The structural fix isn't 'hire more onto the same team'.

questions.q: What happens at ~60+ ICs with a platform team?
options: It becomes a bottleneck, and pods route around it with shadow tooling
questions.explain: Treat thresholds as ranges.

questions.q: What does the choice of split axis (product surface, lifecycle stage, customer segment) determine?
options: What breaks later; there's no universally correct axis, only trade-offs
questions.explain: Each optimises something and costs something.

questions.q: What does governance, done well, do?
options: Provide checkpoints that catch problems while they cost an afternoon, producing evidence not just intentions
questions.explain: Managers need triage, not case law.

questions.q: What triage question should a manager ask?
options: Does it touch credit, employment, health, housing or another protected decision, or the EU or a state with an AI statute? If yes, treat as high-risk
questions.explain: Regardless of the engineering team's technical classification.

questions.q: When should the governance intake checklist be required?
options: Before production, early enough to change course cheaply
questions.explain: It determines the evidence you must produce.

questions.q: Which regimes might apply?
options: EU AI Act, US sectoral rules, state AI laws, GDPR/privacy laws, sector supervisory guidance
questions.explain: Which applies determines what you must be able to show.

questions.q: What is the trap in LLM project timelines?
options: A compelling demo in an afternoon; the gap to production (evals, guardrails, cost control, long-tail inputs) is about 80% of the work
questions.explain: Time to first demo is hours versus weeks for classical ML.

questions.q: How does cost structure differ?
options: Classical: mostly fixed training compute; LLM: variable per-token costs that scale with usage
questions.explain: Budget for usage.

questions.q: What new failure modes does an LLM add?
options: Hallucination, prompt injection and unsafe output, on top of wrong predictions
questions.explain: Evaluation is harder: open-ended outputs often need human or LLM judges.

questions.q: What vendor risk comes with foundation models?
options: Model version changes and deprecations that can change behaviour under you
questions.explain: Dependency is often high.

questions.q: What is the most common strategic mistake in AI hiring?
options: Treating it as one undifferentiated pipeline
questions.explain: Research skills differ from production-shipping skills.

questions.q: If a team struggles to ship and says 'we lack research talent', what's likely wrong?
options: The ratio: most orgs need far more applied, MLOps and data engineering capacity than research
questions.explain: Titles may be right but the ratio wrong.

questions.q: What drives senior ML talent attrition most?
options: A ladder where the only way up is management; build a real dual-track ladder
questions.explain: IC and manager tracks should both progress.

questions.q: How should you anchor hiring?
options: On what the role actually does, not the candidate's title
questions.explain: Titles are inconsistent across companies.

questions.q: When should you build a shared AI platform?
options: When there's measured evidence of duplication cost (e.g. 2+ teams building the same capability); not yet otherwise
questions.explain: Too early solves problems nobody has; too late means invisible reinvention.

questions.q: What is often the better first move than a platform?
options: A shared standard, such as one eval report format
questions.explain: It captures much of the benefit at almost no cost.

questions.q: What should be centralised first?
options: The model/experiment registry, then a shared eval framework, then deployment/serving
questions.explain: Sequence by leverage, not technical interest.

questions.q: Why verify duplication with contracts and onboarding data?
options: To show it's real, not anecdotal
questions.explain: Evidence justifies the investment.

questions.q: How do AI incidents differ from traditional outages?
options: Often quality degradation: the system runs and answers but quietly gets worse, tripping no uptime alert
questions.explain: Monitoring must catch quality, not just availability.

questions.q: Which are AI-specific failure modes?
options: Drift, silent input schema change, feedback-loop degradation, hallucination, bias regression, prompt injection, vendor-side model change
questions.explain: Most produce no error or crash.

questions.q: What defines SEV1 for AI?
options: Active harm to users/customers or ongoing regulatory/legal exposure
questions.explain: Severity reflects quality-based harm, not only downtime.

questions.q: Why does conventional monitoring miss them?
options: Latency, error rate and uptime don't change when output quality degrades
questions.explain: You need quality monitoring.

questions.q: What are the four ROI buckets?
options: Hard cost savings, revenue impact, risk/cost avoidance, soft/strategic value
questions.explain: Keep them separate.

questions.q: How should a credible ROI report treat them?
options: Lead with the first two, include the third with stated assumptions, mention the fourth without pretending it's quantified
questions.explain: Collapsing into 'value created' loses credibility.

questions.q: Net benefit in year 1?
options: Gross benefit − run cost − build cost
questions.explain: Year 2+ drops the one-time build cost.

questions.q: What is the payback period?
options: Time from launch until cumulative net benefit turns positive
questions.explain: Beware inflating soft benefits.

questions.q: What AI-specific vendor risks exist?
options: Model behaviour can change without a version bump you control, usage-based pricing is hard to forecast, and switching costs are higher than they look
questions.explain: Prompts, evals and integrations become entangled with one vendor's model.

questions.q: At what granularity should build/buy/partner be decided?
questions.explain: Build the core recommender, buy LLM API access, partner on niche vision.

questions.q: Which vendor questions matter specifically?
options: Can we pin a model version, and what's the minimum notice before deprecating a model we depend on?
questions.explain: Model versioning transparency and deprecation policy.

questions.q: What favours building?
options: The capability is core to competitive advantage or data can't leave your environment
questions.explain: Buying fits commodity or fast time-to-value.

questions.q: What is a well-built AI CoE?
options: A small, high-leverage standards-and-enablement function with a narrow explicit mandate
questions.explain: It's measured by pod adoption and outcomes, not headcount.

questions.q: What's the early warning sign of a CoE going wrong?
options: Pod leads call it 'the team we have to go through' instead of 'the team that helps us'
questions.explain: It becomes a bottleneck.

questions.q: What's the biggest cause of CoE dysfunction?
options: An ambiguous mandate that was never written down
questions.explain: Get written VP-level sign-off and publish it.

questions.q: What belongs in the mandate?
options: Decisions it makes unilaterally, advises on, builds directly, what's out of scope, and an escalation path
questions.explain: For example final sign-off on high-risk launches.

questions.q: What triggered Ridgeline Analytics' governance project?
options: Starting to sell into the EU
questions.explain: It has four AI systems in production and no dedicated compliance role.

questions.q: Which Ridgeline system is the highest risk tier?
options: The LLM support assistant (Medium-High: customer-facing, EU exposure, account data)
questions.explain: Sales-lead scoring is Low: internal only.

questions.q: Why is the system-of-record inventory central?
options: Every later section depends on it; it's re-tiered quarterly and new systems are added at intake
questions.explain: Add new systems before development starts.

questions.q: What does the framework deliver?
options: A complete deliverable a CEO or board can understand: how the org decides what's safe to build, launch and keep running
questions.explain: It combines modules 1–9.

questions.q: At the executive level, what does AI strategy become?
questions.explain: Over-investing chases hype; under-investing cedes advantage.

questions.q: What's the executive mistake in the positioning matrix?
options: Misplacing a capability: treating a strategic bet as a peripheral efficiency play, or a commodity as strategic
questions.explain: Peripheral and low differentiation means buy, don't build.

questions.q: Describe the three-horizon model.
options: H1 0–12 months efficiency of existing systems; H2 1–3 years new products on proven techniques; H3 3+ years exploratory bets
questions.explain: Each has a different investment character and risk.

questions.q: A core-to-business, high-differentiation capability should be...
options: A strategic bet worth deliberate investment
questions.explain: Core and low differentiation is an efficiency play.

questions.q: What are the three org archetypes?
options: Centralised AI org, embedded model, hybrid hub-and-spoke
questions.explain: The right one depends on whether AI is your product, process or a feature.

questions.q: How do many companies evolve?
options: Start centralised and drift toward hybrid past roughly 3–4 business units with distinct AI needs
questions.explain: Plan for the transition.

questions.q: What does a CAIO reporting to the CEO signal?
options: AI is core strategy, not a support function
questions.explain: Under the CTO signals a technical capability; under CPO a product capability.

questions.q: Which design tensions must be resolved?
options: Centralised versus embedded talent, product-led versus research-led priorities, and business-unit autonomy
questions.explain: They're consistent across AI-first orgs.

questions.q: What is risk-adjusted value?
questions.explain: Probability must be honest and calibrated.

questions.q: A $4.2M project at 50% success versus a $1.7M project at 90%. Which has higher risk-adjusted value?
questions.explain: Verified by calculation.

questions.q: Ranked by risk-adjusted value, how do projects B, C, A and D order?
options: B ($2.10M) > C ($1.68M) > A ($1.53M) > D ($0.90M), different from raw value order B > D > C > A
questions.explain: The risk-adjusted order should drive funding.

questions.q: Should project D (30% success, novel) get funding?
options: A small Horizon-3 exploratory investment, not Horizon-2-scale funding on raw upside alone
questions.explain: It's unproven.

questions.q: What are the two failure modes in disruption communication?
questions.explain: Neither builds trust.

questions.q: What is the credible middle?
options: Be honest about what you know, what you don't yet, and when you'll know more, with a dated commitment
questions.explain: Specific, dated communication.

questions.q: Why does premature alarm backfire?
options: Announcing broad restructuring before specific plans exist triggers fear and attrition
questions.explain: Best people leave first.

questions.q: Why is AI disruption an ongoing condition?
options: Once AI materially changes work, roles keep changing and people watch executives' signals
questions.explain: Handle it honestly and continuously.

questions.q: What should an exposure map be?
options: A live map of jurisdictions you operate in, cross-referenced with your high-risk systems, not a one-time legal memo
questions.explain: The intersection of high-risk system and regulated jurisdiction deserves executive attention first.

questions.q: How should major decisions be made while regulation is still being written?
options: With explicit scenario planning rather than betting on one predicted outcome
questions.explain: Regulatory exposure may change before the system ships.

questions.q: How does the US federal posture differ from the EU's?
options: Sectoral with agency guidance and no single comprehensive law, versus the EU's comprehensive risk-tiered AI Act
questions.explain: US states are increasingly active, e.g. Colorado.

questions.q: What regime does China apply to generative AI?
questions.explain: Other markets range from principles to binding rules.

questions.q: What is the one job of AI board reporting?
options: Give enough accurate signal to ask the right questions and make real decisions
questions.explain: Neither overwhelm with detail nor oversimplify.

questions.q: What are the four standing sections?
options: Strategic positioning, performance, risk and governance, forward look
questions.explain: Quarterly, 4–6 pages plus appendix.

questions.q: A report needing 45 minutes to present has usually...
questions.explain: Choosing board-level versus management-level items is the skill.

questions.q: Which belongs at board level?
options: Portfolio risk-adjusted value, SEV1 incidents, regulatory exposure and talent risk summaries
questions.explain: The test is whether a board member with fiduciary duty would need it.

questions.q: What is culture, per the lesson?
options: What happens when nobody's checking, such as flagging a bad eval or skipping governance under deadline
questions.explain: Frameworks only work if behaviour matches them.

questions.q: How should the culture-practice gap be diagnosed?
options: Honest surveys or structured interviews with ICs, not leadership self-assessment
questions.explain: Leadership and IC views often differ, and the gap itself is diagnostic.

questions.q: What's the most underused lever?
options: Incentive alignment: reviews, promotions and bonuses
questions.explain: Culture statements change nothing if only shipped features are rewarded.

questions.q: Which question reveals psychological safety?
options: Would a junior engineer feel comfortable escalating a senior's skipped eval step?
questions.explain: Also whether bad results are reported as readily as good.

questions.q: What is the most common AI M&A diligence failure?
options: Valuing on a demo and pitch deck without verifying reproducibility and data rights
questions.explain: Those two make the capability worth far less once ownership transfers.

questions.q: What does model reproducibility diligence ask?
options: Can the team retrain their key model from scratch with documented steps?
questions.explain: Otherwise the model is a black box you can't maintain.

questions.q: Why check data rights and provenance?
options: Governance liabilities transfer onto the acquirer's books
questions.explain: The target may lack rights to the training data.

questions.q: Which team risk appears after acquisition?
options: A flight risk once retention packages expire
questions.explain: Integration decisions determine whether value is captured.

questions.q: What does the executive level require beyond technical judgment and team leadership?
options: Capital allocation, board communication and organisational politics at a scale where you can't personally verify most of what you're accountable for
questions.explain: The skills that made you a strong manager are necessary but insufficient.

questions.q: Is the path a simple seniority ladder?
options: No: each step shifts what you optimise for, with specific gaps that stall people
questions.explain: The module maps the progression concretely.

questions.q: Why do people stall at transitions?
options: Specific skill gaps, not lack of effort
questions.explain: Identify and build them deliberately.

questions.q: What's the executive job's central shift?
options: From verifying work yourself to allocating capital and trusting systems and people
questions.explain: You can no longer verify most of it personally.

questions.q: What is Halloway Group's AI budget split across horizons?
Which quadrant is fraud detection?
options: Core, low-differentiation: table stakes every competitor has
questions.explain: Credit-risk underwriting is core and high-differentiation.

questions.q: Underwriting refinement: $4.5M at 85% success. Risk-adjusted value?
What did the board ask for?
options: A complete AI strategy and governance review within one quarter, after a competitor's AI-driven product launch
questions.explain: The capstone integrates strategy, portfolio, governance, org design, culture and board communication.

questions.q: Your CEO asks for a firm delivery date for a new ML feature at kickoff. What should you give?
options: A range tied to explicit checkpoints (e.g. feasibility in 3 weeks) that narrows as evidence arrives
questions.explain: AI duration depends on questions only answered by doing the work.

questions.q: A proof of concept shows the approach can't reach the quality bar. How should you treat it?
options: As a reason to add staff
As the project doing its job: it prevented a far more expensive production failure; apply the kill criteria
questions.explain: Budget kill criteria at the end of stages 1–3.

questions.q: The vendor's demo is impressive. What do you do before buying?
options: Run a pilot on a sample of your own data and check cost at your scale, data handling, p95/p99 latency, SLA and lock-in
questions.explain: Demos run on best-case examples.

questions.q: A dashboard shows accuracy, latency and uptime all green, yet users have stopped using the tool. What's missing?
options: An adoption metric: weekly active use of the intended population and whether the business metric moved
questions.explain: The costliest failure is a model that works and is ignored.

questions.q: Offline model accuracy improved but engagement dropped. Where's the gap?
options: Between the model and product metric layers: the team optimised a number that doesn't move the outcome
questions.explain: Every project needs a metric per layer and how movement propagates.

questions.q: Project A: $1.7M at 90%. B: $4.2M at 50%. C: $2.1M at 80%. D: $3.0M at 30%. Which has the highest risk-adjusted value?
questions.explain: Value × probability of success. Verified by calculation.

questions.q: Which cost line do AI budgets most often under-plan?
options: Usage-driven and non-modelling costs, since modelling is usually the smallest line; use staged funding
questions.explain: Commit money in tranches tied to decision points.

questions.q: A model is retrained on customer data collected only to deliver a service. What governance question is breached?
options: Purpose: data collected for one purpose isn't automatically usable for training and may need a different legal basis
questions.explain: It's the most common reason a finished model can't ship.

questions.q: A hiring manager says 'we need more research scientists to ship faster'. What's your diagnosis?
options: Likely the wrong ratio: most orgs need far more applied, MLOps and data engineering capacity than research
questions.explain: Anchor hiring to what the role does.

questions.q: Two pods built separate eval harnesses. What's the first move?
options: Introduce a shared standard (e.g. one eval report format) before a full platform, and check the duplication is measured
questions.explain: A platform comes when measured duplication justifies it.

questions.q: A deployed model quietly degrades: no errors, uptime 100%. Which monitoring catches it?
options: Quality monitoring for drift, input schema changes and outcome metrics, not just latency and errors
questions.explain: Most AI failures trip no conventional alert.

questions.q: A foundation-model vendor updates the model and your outputs change. What contract/term would have helped?
options: Version pinning and a minimum deprecation notice period
questions.explain: Model behaviour can change without a version bump you control.

questions.q: A customer-facing LLM assistant sells into the EU and handles account data. What tier is sensible?
options: Higher risk (e.g. medium-high): customer-facing, EU exposure, account data; run governance intake before production
questions.explain: Treat decisions touching protected categories or EU/state AI laws as high-risk.

questions.q: The board asks for an AI update. What should the report contain?
options: A short standing report: strategic positioning, performance vs projection, risk and governance, and forward look
questions.explain: Choose what's board-worthy versus management-level.

questions.q: Leaders announce 'AI will never cost jobs' before plans exist. What's the failure mode?
options: False reassurance (the opposite is premature alarm); be honest about what's known and give a dated commitment
questions.explain: Neither builds trust.

questions.q: Reviews and promotions reward only shipped features. What happens to responsible-AI practices?
options: They erode, because incentives beat statements; add explicit quality, safety and governance criteria
questions.explain: Incentive alignment is the most underused lever.

questions.q: You're acquiring an AI startup based on its demo. What two things must you verify?
questions.explain: They're the items most likely to make the capability worth less than represented.

questions.q: A CoE is described by pod leads as 'the team we have to go through'. What's wrong?
options: It has drifted into an approval gate; refocus on a written narrow mandate, advisory tooling and pod outcomes
questions.explain: Ambiguity of mandate is the biggest cause of CoE dysfunction.

questions.q: Which is the right first sequence when a platform is justified?
options: Model/experiment registry, then shared eval framework, then deployment/serving
questions.explain: Sequence by leverage, not technical interest.

questions.q: A company runs 11 AI systems across three business units and drifts from one central AI team. What structure often fits at scale?
options: Hybrid hub-and-spoke: a central hub for platform, standards and governance with embedded spokes
questions.explain: Past ~3–4 business units with distinct needs, most drift to hybrid.
